transcript: Doctor: Sir, I'm Dr. Okafor. Can you tell me what happened? Patient: I was playing pickup football at the park and I went to catch a pass and landed on my right arm. I felt a pop and the pain was immediate. Doctor: On a scale of one to ten how is the pain right now? Patient: Eight, maybe nine when I try to move it. Doctor: I can see some deformity in the mid forearm area. Can you wiggle your fingers for me? Patient: Yeah I can move them but it hurts. Doctor: Good, that tells me your nerve function is intact. Let me check your pulse at the wrist. Radial pulse is strong and your capillary refill is brisk, that's all good signs. I'm going to order an X-ray of the right forearm. In the meantime we'll get you some pain medication. Nurse: Doctor, X-ray results are back. Patient: What does it show? Doctor: You have fractures of both the radius and ulna in the mid shaft, what we call a both bone forearm fracture. The good news is the fragments aren't significantly displaced. Patient: Do I need surgery? Doctor: Given the minimal displacement I think we can manage this with a long arm cast. If we see any shifting on follow up X-rays we might need to reconsider. I'm going to reduce the fracture with some sedation, apply a splint today, and you'll follow up with orthopedics in one week for casting. You'll need to keep it elevated above your heart as much as possible and ice around the splint for swelling. I'll prescribe a short course of pain medication. Patient: How long until it heals? Doctor: Typically six to eight weeks in the cast, then physical therapy to regain range of motion. Any questions? Patient: No, let's get this taken care of. Doctor: Alright, the nurse will get your sedation started.
